claim:
Let \(1<p<\infty\), and let \(X_p=(\mathbb R^2,N_p)\) be the real Day--James plane
\[
N_p(u,v)=
\begin{cases}
\bigl(|u|^p+|v|^p\bigr)^{1/p},&uv\ge0,\\
|u|+|v|,&uv\le0.
\end{cases}
\]
For the Baronti--Casini--Papini constant
\[
A_2(X_p)=\sup_{x,y\in S_{X_p}}\frac{N_p(x+y)+N_p(x-y)}2,
\]
the known value is
\[
A_2(X_p)=1+2^{1/p-1}.
\]
Moreover, the complete equality set is rigid:
\[
\frac{N_p(x+y)+N_p(x-y)}2=1+2^{1/p-1}
\]
holds if and only if
\[
\{x,y\}=\{\varepsilon e_1,\delta e_2\}
\qquad
\text{for some }\varepsilon,\delta\in\{-1,1\}.
\]
Thus, for every \(1<p<\infty\), the only \(A_2\)-maximizing pairs are the two coordinate-axis unit vectors, up to order and independent sign changes of the two vectors.

correctness.rationale: The exact-object source proves the sharp bound and supplies the two branch inequalities. For \(p>1\), the same-sign \(\ell_p\) arc is strictly convex. In the crossing branch, equality below the threshold would require equality in Minkowski and a positive crossing defect, which is impossible; equality above the threshold forces \(a+d=2\), hence \(a=d=1\) and \(b=c=0\). Every nonextreme sphere point lies inside an opposite-sign \(\ell_1\)-edge. Convex equality there would force both axis endpoints to maximize with one common extreme partner, contradicting the extreme-point classification. The axis pairs attain directly.
risks: Strict convexity is essential, so the endpoint p=1 is excluded.
No assertion is made for general t or tau in the James-type family.

value.rationale: The Day--James \(\ell_p-\ell_1\) family is a classical infinite family used for exact Banach-space geometric constants, and \(A_2\) is a standard triangle/perimeter parameter tied to uniform nonsquareness. The scalar value alone leaves open whether sharpness is isolated, face-supported, or distributed along curved arcs. Proving that every sharp pair is forced onto the two coordinate axes gives a complete structural answer for the whole \(1<p<\infty\) family. The result is therefore a natural rigidity theorem rather than a routine re-evaluation of the known constant.
risks: The theorem refines one classical constant rather than introducing a new invariant.
No quantitative stability modulus for near-maximizers is claimed.
